executive_summary: EUR/USD closed at 1.11674 on 30 October 2026, which means 1 euro buys 1.11674 dollars. The pair is down 0.67% over one month, 3.17% over three months, 4.75% over six months and 3.62% over a year. It closes at the 4th percentile of its 52-week closing range (1.11362 to 1.19773), and the intraday low of 1.11068 was set on 29 October. The bilateral story is an energy terms-of-trade shock layered on French fiscal stress. Brent at US$117.64 and Dutch TTF gas near EUR100/MWh cut euro-area income, while the US, a net energy exporter, gains. Meanwhile the 137.5bp policy gap (ECB 2.50% against a Fed midpoint of 3.875%) holds steady, and neither central bank decides before 9 December. The bilateral reading adds two things that neither currency view shows alone. First, ECB December pricing (quoted from 67% to 84%) is less settled than Fed pricing (77-85%), so the euro leg is the one more likely to disappoint. Second, the futures funding premium of 145.9bp, above the policy gap, shows the market expects no narrowing. The tactical stance is Bearish (score -0.37, conviction 3, confidence 55%) with a four-week base case of 1.1050. The strategic stance is Bearish (score -0.23, conviction 2, confidence 52%) with a base case of 1.0950 by end-April 2027. The main caveat is that both views depend on breaking a 200-week average at 1.11088 that is rising about 6.5 pips a week. That has to happen against a legacy speculative euro short of 143,900 contracts, which is stretched enough to squeeze 150-250 pips on a soft US payroll print or a Hormuz headline.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On GDP-based PPP the euro is deeply cheap: fair EUR/USD is about 1.4085, a 20.7% euro discount (equivalently, the dollar is 26.1% rich). The real effective measures tell a less extreme story: the BIS real broad index for the euro is 103.27, the 67th percentile of its range since January 2024, while the dollar's real index is 107.11, only the 21st percentile. In real trade-weighted terms, then, the euro is not cheap and the dollar is not expensive. The bilateral gap is a nominal one sustained by a 137.5bp rate gap and an energy-importer discount. What the current level prices is a persistent euro risk premium for the energy shock and the French spread. It does not price mean reversion to PPP. That reversion has historically taken years and has no catalyst inside six months.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy differential is -137.5bp against the euro: an ECB deposit rate of 2.50% against a Fed target midpoint of 3.875%, both as of 27 October. At the two-year point the gap is wider, about 153-159bp in the dollar's favour (US 2-year 4.61% on 29 October against a Schatz of 3.02-3.08% on 30 October), although it narrowed about 7bp in October as the ECB turned hawkish. The listed futures calendar spread pays a 145.9bp annualised premium (observed 29 October). That is above the policy gap, so once the cross-currency basis is mixed in, the market expects no narrowing. Neither central bank decides inside the four-week window. The Fed's next decision, with projections, is 9 December and the ECB's, with staff projections, is 17 December, so the tactical channel is how the data reprices each bank. The US calendar matters more here: payrolls on 6 November and CPI on 10 November can move December Fed pricing of 77-85%. The euro-area HICP flash on 4 November is expected in line at 3.9%. ECB December pricing is quoted anywhere from 67% (LSEG, after the meeting) to about 84% (StoneX). That makes the euro leg the less settled side and the one more likely to disappoint. The effect works through carry and the front-end gap: holding the euro against the dollar costs roughly 13 pips a month, with no scheduled event in the window that could close the gap.

tactical.what_is_priced: Both December hikes are mostly priced, so the market expects the differential to end the year unchanged, and a futures premium about 8bp above the policy gap even implies slight widening. The tactical edge is that ECB pricing is less settled than Fed pricing, so a euro-side disappointment is the more likely repricing before the 9 and 17 December decisions.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the question is whether the differential narrows, and both curves price more tightening than their banks have signalled. The Fed's market path runs near 4.7% by September 2027 against a September median dot of 4.1%, a gap of 50-60bp. The ECB is priced for roughly 75bp of further hikes, while the sell side clusters on one hike to 2.75% and then a pause: Rabobank expects a pause after December, Deutsche Bank calls December probably the end, and UBS sees a 3.00% terminal in early 2027. If both curves move back to what their banks have signalled, the Fed's repricing is larger, which would narrow the expected differential by roughly 25-35bp, a marginal positive for the euro. Against that, the carry stays negative for the euro throughout, at 112.5-137.5bp across plausible outcomes. The sequence also matters. The Fed's 9 December projections come eight days before the ECB's 17 December projections, so higher dots would confirm the Fed path before the ECB speaks. A Fed hike with a hold signal followed by an ECB hike framed as the last leaves the gap at 137.5bp. A Fed hold with an ECB hike would narrow it to 112.5bp. Over-pricing on both sides offsets an unchanged carry deficit, so the honest strategic reading is Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth differential is wide and favours the dollar. US third-quarter GDP grew 3.4% annualised (0.83% q/q, 2.07% y/y) against 0.4% q/q and 1.3% y/y in the euro area. The October flash composite PMI was 57.6 in the US against 51.9 in the euro area, a 5.7-point gap that widened as the euro-area reading fell from 53.1. The inflation mix differs in a way that matters for policy. Euro-area headline HICP is 3.8%, but core is only 2.5% and the rise is energy cost-push, with wages tracking 2.5-2.8%. US core PCE is 3.1%, with services and ISM prices paid at 77.9 pointing to second-round pressure. So the US combines strong activity with sticky core inflation, while the euro area combines softening activity with an energy-driven headline. The two business cycles are in different phases: a late-cycle expansion in the US and a stagflationary squeeze in Europe, where unemployment has risen to 6.5%. The data most likely to move the pair is asymmetric. Weak US payrolls are the soft spot (September +29,000 with 60,000 of downward revisions), so the 6 November report is the main upside risk for the pair, while the 4 November HICP flash is expected in line. On balance the four-week data flow is more likely to confirm the growth gap than to close it.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the euro area faces a real-income squeeze: headline inflation of 3.8%, which UBS sees peaking at 4.1% in January 2027, against wage growth of 2.5-2.8%. Bank lending growth is slowing (4.2% to firms in September) and credit standards tightened in the third quarter. France contracted 0.1% in Q3 and its flash PMI is 48.4. The US slows from a much higher base. The Atlanta Fed tracks Q4 at 3.2-3.3%, and even a fall to 2% would leave US growth ahead of the euro area's expected 0.1-0.2% q/q. The US weak spot is the labour market. Three-month average payrolls are about 51,000 and real hourly earnings are down 0.7% y/y, so a rise in unemployment to 4.5% would narrow the gap quickly and shift the Fed. Germany's fiscal expansion of EUR117.5bn in investment supports euro-area growth, but mainly after this horizon. The cycle gap therefore keeps favouring the dollar, at lower confidence than tactically because of the US labour-market tail.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: EUR/USD is normally a low risk-sensitivity pair, but in this regime both of the euro's risk channels are negative and both are active. The first is energy: the US has said strikes on Iran are possible after the 3 November midterms, and two tankers were hit near Hormuz on 29-30 October. The second is French sovereign stress. Credit shows the asymmetry: the euro high-yield spread widened 54bp in a month to 3.48% (peaking at 3.64% on 23 October), while the US investment-grade spread is 89bp and US high yield 326bp, up 18bp. The VIX rose from 17.2 to about 20 intraday on 30 October on an AI-led equity sell-off. The dollar's haven response to that equity shock was weak, which limits how much a generic risk-off helps the dollar against the euro. An energy-led risk-off is different: it hits euro-area terms of trade directly while the US is a net energy exporter, so for this pair the escalation tail is euro-negative. Our estimates put a US strike within four weeks at 20-35% and a Hormuz deal at about 15%, so the skew is negative for the pair, at low confidence.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk regime is two-sided for the pair. Escalation in the Gulf would deepen Europe's energy shock and is euro-negative. A settlement would remove the energy premium and is strongly euro-positive: talks resumed in Tehran with Qatari, Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish involvement. A deeper US-led equity correction is the third branch. It would hit US assets first, and ING flags low hedge ratios on US holdings, so a US-centred de-risking could produce dollar selling through rising hedge ratios rather than a haven bid. That branch is euro-positive. US credit at 89bp investment grade is tight enough to widen materially. Weighting escalation, muddle-through and settlement together with an equity-correction tail, the net effect is within the error of the estimate, so the factor is Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The terms-of-trade differential is the most euro-specific negative in the pair. Dutch TTF gas traded at EUR100/MWh on 28 October for the first time since December 2022, with EU storage about 75% full and Germany's about 60% going into winter. Brent closed at US$117.64 on 30 October. The euro area is a net importer of both. The US is a net energy exporter with Henry Hub gas at only US$2.76, so the same shock that drains euro-area income improves the US terms of trade. The euro-area trade balance has already turned: an August deficit of EUR16.1bn, the largest since January 2023, with petroleum imports up 20.7% y/y. The current-account surplus fell to EUR9bn in August from EUR27bn in July. Bilateral goods trade still favours the euro: IMF DOTS shows euro-area exports to the US of USD521.1bn against imports of USD327.8bn in 2024, a USD193.3bn surplus, and August exports to the US rose 18.5% y/y under the 15% tariff ceiling. But that surplus is a stable level, not a changing one, while the energy bill is rising now. For the next four weeks, with winter demand starting and storage below normal, the factor is Bearish at the highest tactical confidence of the ten.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Structurally, the external balances still favour the euro in level terms: a euro-area current-account surplus of 1.5% of GDP against a US deficit of 3.0%, a US net international investment position of -USD22.42tn that deteriorated USD1.15tn in one quarter, and a bilateral goods surplus with the US of USD193.3bn. The direction of change, however, favours the dollar over a one-to-three-month horizon. The euro-area surplus has fallen from EUR290bn to EUR250bn on a 12-month basis, and August's EUR9bn monthly figure implies something closer to 1.0% of GDP by early 2027 if gas stays near current levels. The US deficit is also widening (a September advance goods deficit of USD134.9bn), but it is financed by private inflows of USD257.8bn in August at Treasury yields near 5%. Valuation is the main offset: GDP-based PPP puts fair EUR/USD near 1.41, a 20-26% euro undervaluation, and the BIS real effective dollar rate is at only the 21st percentile of its two-year range. Those are multi-year anchors with no catalyst inside the horizon. Net, the energy-driven erosion of the euro's external cushion outweighs a level advantage that markets already know, so the factor is Bearish at moderate confidence.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: EUR: large net importer of oil and natural gas; TTF gas and Brent are the key prices. Oil up is negative (-EUR) and TTF up is negative (-EUR) under the direction rules. The petroleum import bill rose 20.7% y/y in August.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: USD: net exporter of crude, refined products and LNG, with domestic gas (Henry Hub US$2.76) insulated from TTF. Higher oil improves US terms of trade and recycles petrodollars into US assets, a mild positive (+USD).
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1: Oil up 10% means EUR negative (-) under the direction rules, because the euro area is a net importer, while the US terms of trade improve mildly (+) as a net exporter. Step 2: TTF gas up means EUR negative (-) under the rules, while the US is largely unaffected because Henry Hub is decoupled and higher global LNG prices help US exporters (mild +). Step 3: Netting the two legs, both commodity channels push the euro down and the dollar flat-to-up, so the effects add rather than cancel: higher energy prices mean the pair falls. Step 4: The gas channel is larger than oil for the euro because of below-normal storage and TTF at about three times pre-war levels.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair falls: the euro-area import bill and real-income squeeze worsen while US terms of trade improve, adding to the external-balance and growth headwinds for EUR/USD.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair rises: the euro area's energy bill eases and the ECB's stagflation dilemma softens, while the US loses a modest terms-of-trade gain. The effect is larger if TTF falls with it.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Dutch TTF natural gas, because the euro area's winter storage gap makes gas the commodity with the largest asymmetric effect between the two legs.

The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October by 10-2, with Cook and Hammack voting to hike. Its statement said the Committee 'will deliver price stability', though Chair Warsh rejects forward guidance outside a crisis and declined to pre-judge December. Both banks' December pricing broadly matches the signal. The ECB's messaging was mixed, though: Rabobank notes the ECB sees no extra second-round effects and that internal estimates of the drag from higher bond yields point to a pause after December. The next communication tests inside the window are the FOMC minutes on 18 November and the ECB Account on 26 November. Neither is likely to move pricing much, so the factor is Neutral.

Lagarde has announced she will step down in early February 2027, and a successor search is under way during a supply shock. FXStreet notes that any doubt about the central bank's independence during the handover could weigh on confidence in the euro. Rabobank and Deutsche Bank read the ECB as hoping to pause after December, and the September projections already have core HICP at 2.6% in 2027 and 2.3% in 2028, which does not require the 3.25% terminal implied by pricing. On the Fed side, the market path near 4.7% for 2027 sits above the 4.1% median dot, so the Fed also has dovish-repricing risk. But its credibility is intact: it hiked in September, two governors are voting for more, and the Treasury Secretary has said further hikes would not necessarily be mistakes. The 9 December projections, the first under the no-guidance approach, come before the ECB's 17 December staff projections, so the Fed sets the tone. The euro faces both a leadership-transition discount and a guidance-pricing gap, while the Fed faces only the latter, so the factor is Bearish at low confidence.

Further euro-specific events follow: a union strike on 5 November, the whole-budget vote on 17 November, where Article 49.3 would trigger an immediate censure motion, and S&P's review of France (A+ stable) on 27 November. Prediction markets gave only a 44.5% chance of a French budget by year-end. On the US side, the midterm result is largely priced. A Democratic House could revive trade-policy risk, which ING sees as dollar-negative, and the government funding deadline of 11 December falls just outside the window. A strike on Iran would hurt the euro through energy far more than the dollar. A Hormuz deal (about 15%) is the only clearly euro-positive event. The probability-weighted event map is negative for the pair.

The dominant euro-side risks are directional and negative, while the US-side risks are uncertain in sign, so the factor is Bearish at slightly lower confidence than tactically.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar liquidity is tightening at the margin into year-end, which acts on this pair directly through the quote leg. Reserve balances fell USD68.8bn in the week to 28 October to a USD2,893.8bn weekly average, as the Treasury General Account rose to USD1,015.6bn, well above Treasury's USD850bn end-December target. SOFR was 3.94% on 29 October, 4bp above interest on reserves of 3.90%. The balance sheet is flat at about USD6.75tn and reserve-management purchases have been zero since mid-August, so nothing is offsetting the drain. There is no stress: standing-repo use was USD6m, central-bank swap lines USD156m, and the euro-area banking system is not dollar-constrained. The futures funding premium of 145.9bp, against a 137.5bp policy gap, implies at most a small dollar funding premium of about 8bp including expected policy moves. A free 3-month cross-currency basis is not available to confirm it. Seasonal year-end dollar demand from late November adds to the cost of dollar funding for euro-area banks. The factor is therefore mildly dollar-positive over four weeks, Bearish for the pair.

Rates, growth and dollar liquidity together contribute -0.29, so the call rests mainly on the policy gap, the US growth lead and year-end funding rather than on any single high-conviction euro-specific event. tactical.rationale: At tactical weights, Policy & Rates (0.24), Inflation & Growth (0.18) and USD Liquidity (0.11) carry more than half the score, and all three are Bearish for the pair. The 137.5bp policy gap is stable, neither central bank decides inside four weeks, and the futures funding premium of 145.9bp implies no expected narrowing. The confidence-weighted score is -0.37: seven Bearish factors, one Bullish and two Neutral. The two dossiers reinforce each other. The euro dossier is Bearish on energy, French fiscal stress and an ECB it sees as over-priced. The dollar dossier is Bullish on a hiking Fed, 3.4% GDP growth and tightening year-end liquidity. The bilateral additions sharpen this. Energy is a pure differential: the euro area imports the TTF and Brent shock that improves US terms of trade, while a bilateral goods surplus of USD193.3bn is a stable level that does not offset a rising energy bill. ECB December pricing is quoted between 67% and 84%, while Fed pricing is a firmer 77-85%, so the euro leg has more room to disappoint before the 9 and 17 December decisions. What is priced is a December hike from both banks. Our edge is that the four-week data calendar (HICP flash 4 November, payrolls 6 November, CPI 10 November) is more likely to confirm the US growth lead than to narrow it, and that euro-negative events (a post-midterm strike on Iran, the 17 November French budget vote, the 27 November S&P review) are not priced. The path of least resistance is therefore a lower euro against the dollar over four weeks. The main risk to that path is a squeeze from a legacy speculative euro short of 143,900 contracts, beyond its historical extreme. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because no factor exceeds 60 confidence, the score depends on breadth, and crowded positioning makes the path vulnerable to a sharp reversal on a soft US payroll print or a Hormuz headline. It is not 2 because the energy, fiscal and rate channels work independently of each other and are all active at once.

EUR/NOK combines a 200bp carry pick-up with the direct gas terms-of-trade channel, and EUR/GBP offers better carry relative to volatility ahead of a likely BoE hike on 5 November. Among dollar longs, EUR/USD ranks alongside USD/CHF, which has wider carry but a haven risk if Gulf tensions escalate. EUR/USD offers the greatest liquidity and the most direct exposure to the euro-specific energy and French channels.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights Policy & Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.16), Guidance (0.12) and USD Liquidity (0.12) dominate. Only External Balance and Guidance give a directional signal, both Bearish for the pair, which produces a net score of -0.23. External Balance carries most of the euro-specific weight. The euro area's 12-month current-account surplus has slipped from 1.8% to 1.5% of GDP and is heading towards 1% if gas stays near three times pre-war levels, while the US, a net energy exporter, gains on its terms of trade even as its own deficit widens. Growth adds a real-wage squeeze and tighter euro-area credit against a US expansion that is slowing from 3.4%. The dossiers partly conflict here. The euro dossier is strongly Bearish, but the dollar dossier is only Neutral strategically, because the Fed is over-priced by 50-60bp against its dots and peers are hiking. That is why Policy & Rates is Neutral rather than Bearish in the bilateral view: if both curves move back to what their banks have signalled, the Fed's correction is larger and the differential narrows modestly. What is priced is an unchanged differential and a contained energy shock. Our edge is that the erosion of the euro's external cushion and the ECB leadership handover are not in the price. The path of least resistance is a modestly weaker euro, tested first by the Fed projections on 9 December and then the ECB staff projections on 17 December, with the French budget deadline the same day. Conviction is 2: the heaviest factor is Neutral, valuation (PPP fair value near 1.41) and rising dollar hedge ratios are real offsets, and a US labour-market crack or a Hormuz settlement would remove most of the score. The view is wrong if TTF and the French spread fall together, or if the Fed signals a hold through 2027 while the ECB keeps hiking.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically the euro ranks 10th of 11 in its dossier while the dollar ranks only 6th, so the strategic EUR/USD short rests on euro weakness rather than dollar strength. Against surplus currencies such as JPY, SEK, CHF and NOK, the dollar screens weaker over one to three months. Short EUR/NOK and short EUR/CHF therefore express the euro-specific energy and French channels without relying on the dollar. Among euro crosses, EUR/USD ranks behind EUR/NOK but ahead of EUR/JPY, where Japan's larger energy import exposure offsets the euro's weakness.

consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The Reuters poll was taken in early October, before TTF gas reached EUR100/MWh on 28 October, before the OAT-Bund spread hit a 15-year high, before two Fed governors dissented for a hike and before Lagarde announced her departure. It is anchored on a euro-area outlook without a winter gas squeeze or a leadership transition. Consensus also treats ECB hikes as euro-supportive. We weigh the external-balance factor more heavily: the ECB is tightening into a terms-of-trade shock that erodes the current-account surplus, and analysts including Rabobank and Deutsche Bank expect a pause after December, below the roughly 75bp priced. Finally, many forecasters lean on PPP fair value near 1.25-1.41, which we treat as a multi-year anchor with no catalyst inside the horizon.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the euro weakens while consensus expects gains, a short EUR/USD position collects both the spot move and about 13 pips a month of carry: +117 pips tactically and +300 pips against the six-month forward strategically.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If consensus is right, the most likely trigger is energy relief from a US-Iran settlement or a soft run of US labour data. That would meet a legacy speculative euro short of 143,900 contracts, so the loss would come early and fast through short-covering rather than gradually. A move to 1.15 costs 333 pips on spot, or 250 pips against the forward.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Both horizons are Bearish, but on different drivers and with weaker conviction strategically (tactical score -0.37, conviction 3; strategic score -0.23, conviction 2). Tactically, the rate gap, the US growth lead, year-end dollar liquidity and a cluster of dated euro-negative events dominate, with crowded speculative shorts the only offset. Strategically, the policy factor turns Neutral because both curves over-price their central banks, the Fed by more. USD Liquidity turns Neutral as the TGA declines, so the signal narrows to external balance, ECB guidance and growth.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 9 December Fed decision with projections followed by the 17 December ECB decision with staff projections. Higher Fed dots together with an ECB hike framed as the last would reinforce both horizons. A Fed hold signal followed by an ECB hike with guidance for more would turn the strategic view Neutral.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The tactical and strategic views point the same way, so squeezes driven by crowded speculative positioning are better treated as opportunities to build the strategic view than as signals to reverse it. Holding through forwards, where carry accrues to a dollar long, is preferred, while the December projection rounds are the dated tests. catalysts.rationale: A Democratic House is about 94% priced, so the US result matters mainly because it opens the window the White House set for possible strikes on Iran, which would hit euro-area energy terms of trade far harder than the US. Consensus is 3.9% headline after 3.8%, with core the swing variable. A core print well above 2.5% would firm December ECB pricing, which is quoted anywhere from 67% to 84%, and support the euro. An energy-driven headline with flat core would confirm the stagflationary split that weighs on the pair through growth.

Consensus is +55,000 with unemployment at 4.2% after a weak September (+29,000, -60,000 revisions). This is the single release most able to move December Fed pricing of 77-85%. A negative print would cut it sharply and trigger euro short-covering, while a firm print confirms the growth and rate gap against the euro.

September core CPI ran at a 3.4% three-month annualised pace, and core PCE is 3.1%. A repeat would cement the December Fed hike and keep the two-year differential near 155bp in the dollar's favour, while a soft print would narrow the gap that drives the pair.

catalysts.rationale: Prediction markets gave a budget by year-end only 44.5%, and use of Article 49.3 would trigger an immediate censure motion. catalysts.event: FOMC minutes of the 27-28 October meeting
catalysts.rationale: The minutes will show how many participants beyond Cook and Hammack favoured an immediate hike. Wording such as 'many' or 'most' would push December pricing towards 90% and reinforce the dollar's carry advantage before the 9 December projections, which matters more for this pair than for most because the dollar is the higher-yielding leg.

catalysts.event: ECB Account of the October monetary policy meeting
catalysts.rationale: The Account will show how close the Governing Council came to hiking and whether a terminal rate was discussed. A hawkish tone would firm December pricing at the less settled end of its 67-84% range, while signs of a desire to pause after December would confirm the guidance gap that weighs on the euro strategically.

catalysts.event: S&P Global review of France (A+ stable)
catalysts.rationale: Moody's affirmed Aa3 with a negative outlook on 23 October, conditional on a deficit-reducing budget. A negative outlook from S&P after a contested budget vote would widen the French spread and deepen the euro-specific fiscal premium in the pair, with no equivalent dollar event in the window.

catalysts.event: Federal Reserve FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: A hike to 4.00-4.25% is 77-85% priced. The projections decide whether the market's 2027 path near 4.7% survives against a 4.1% median dot. Higher dots would widen the expected differential against the euro, while a hike with a clear hold signal would start the narrowing that keeps the strategic rates factor Neutral. This round comes eight days before the ECB's and sets the tone.

catalysts.event: Expiry of the continuing resolution funding the US government
catalysts.rationale: A lapse in funding would delay US data and raise fiscal and term-premium risk on US assets, which in this regime tends to weigh on the dollar rather than support it. catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision with staff projections; French constitutional budget deadline
catalysts.rationale: A hike to 2.75% is broadly expected. The same day, missing France's constitutional deadline would push the budget towards ordinance or a stopgap law, adding to the euro's fiscal premium.

assumptions: The price analysis uses daily open, high, low and close prices for 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is the 30 October close of 1.11674.

Moving averages, the 200-week average and its slope, and the support and resistance zones are computed over the full stored history: 4,736 weekday sessions from 2008-08-26 to 2026-10-30, including 949 weekly and 275 monthly bars. No weekend bars are included, so every N-day window is a genuine N-trading-day window.
Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 63 pips. Zone distances are measured from spot to the zone midpoint.

The valuation date of 1 November is a Sunday, so the only gap between the spot date and the valuation date is a weekend with no sessions. Early-November web quotes near 1.118-1.12 are noted as context but not used as spot.
Policy rates are as of 27 October 2026: ECB deposit 2.50%, Fed midpoint 3.875%.

The 10-year yields of 3.47% (Germany) and 4.99% (US), a -152bp differential, are September monthly averages and are not quoted as live levels. Late-October daily yields come from the two currency dossiers.

The futures funding premium of 145.9bp (observed 29 October) is the annualised November/December euro futures spread. It combines the interest differential with the cross-currency basis and is not reported as the policy differential. Forward points apply that premium on an actual/360 basis.

Implied volatility, risk reversals and butterflies are CME at-the-money and 25-delta quotes observed 29 October, at 35.7, 98.7 and 189.6 days. The 98.7-day reading of 6.18% is used as the three-month figure. Where the euro dossier cites a one-month risk reversal of -0.61 vols from 28 October, the 29 October reading of -0.30 is used.
The one-month implied-vol percentile rests on 41 observations since 23 August, not a full year.
December ECB hike pricing differs by source and time, from about 67% (LSEG after the meeting) to about 84% (StoneX), and the range is reported.

Event probabilities for a US strike on Iran (20-35%), a French censure and a Hormuz deal are the dossiers' estimates and differ between them, so ranges are used. Scenario, invalidator and conviction-ladder probabilities are our own estimates.
Bilateral goods trade figures are IMF DOTS 2024 values used as stated. Default factor weights apply on both horizons.
No factor stance other than Market Structure & Volatility rests on how EUR/USD has recently traded. Chart levels set entries, stops, targets and invalidators only.
The strategic analysis covers the one-to-six-month horizon. The factor reasoning focuses on the one-to-three-month window, and scenario targets run to end-April 2027.
No public option-barrier data or free three-month cross-currency basis was available. The 1.1100 strike interest cited is from a published bank trade recommendation.
The 52-week percentile in market_context uses the intraday range (1.11068 to 1.20656, 6th percentile); on closes the range is 1.11362 to 1.19773 and spot sits at the 4th percentile.
